es: Tomar notas de una charla breve y resumirlas con tres ideas principales, dos detalles y una conclusión, atribuyendo lo dicho y sin inventar datos.

teaching.en: A good lecturer will draw attention to the turning points, so listen for signals such as first, however and in short, and keep track of how many points she promises.
teaching.es: Un buen conferenciante llamará la atención sobre los puntos de giro, así que escucha señales como first, however e in short, y lleva la cuenta de cuántos puntos promete.
teaching.explanationEs: Keep track of = llevar la cuenta; las señales del orador (first, however, in short) marcan la estructura que debes apuntar.
segments: A good lecturer will draw attention to the turning points, so listen for signals such
as first, however and in short, and keep track of how many points she promises.

teaching.en: According to the lecturer, a key point is that shade cools streets; she went on to give a telling detail: five degrees.
teaching.es: Según la conferenciante, un punto clave es que la sombra refresca las calles; continuó dando un detalle revelador: cinco grados.
teaching.explanationEs: According to atribuye la idea; went on to + verbo añade un dato concreto que respalda el punto.

streets; she went on to give a telling detail: five degrees.

teaching.en: Sensible students jot down keywords and numbers, leaving out whole sentences, because the lecturer will not wait for them.
teaching.es: Los estudiantes sensatos anotan rápido palabras clave y cifras, sin frases enteras, porque el conferenciante no esperará.
teaching.explanationEs: Jot down = anotar de prisa y en pocas palabras; take notes es la expresión general para tomar apuntes.

teaching.en: A recurring theme, such as how firms recruit people, links the three points that the lecturer outlined, so note it once.
teaching.es: Un tema recurrente, como la forma en que las empresas captan personal, une los tres puntos que expuso el conferenciante, así que anótalo una vez.
teaching.explanationEs: Outlined + número de puntos anuncia la estructura; a recurring theme conecta ideas repartidas.

teaching.en: By way of illustration, she described one street where two thousand trees were planted; you can summarise it in a single line.

teaching.explanationEs: By way of illustration introduce un ejemplo; summarise = resumir (resume en inglés significa «reanudar»).

teaching.en: When you summarise, report what was said, not what you think, and close with in short followed by one sentence.
teaching.es: Cuando resumes, cuenta lo que se dijo, no lo que piensas, y cierra con in short seguido de una frase.
teaching.explanationEs: Un resumen fiel separa lo dicho de tu opinión y termina con la conclusión.

prompt.es: ¿Qué debe ir principalmente en tus notas durante una charla?

choices.text: Every sentence exactly as the lecturer says it.
Your own opinion of each idea as it is mentioned.
Numbers, names and the main point of each section.

feedback.es: Con un orador rápido, lo útil son las cifras, los nombres y la idea de cada parte; copiar frases enteras te hace perder el hilo.

hint.es: Piensa en lo que podrás reconstruir después con pocas palabras.

origin.text: You are listening to a twenty-minute talk on shared bikes. The lecturer speaks quickly, gives many figures and names, and moves on before you have finished writing.

prompt.es: Completa: «Según la conferenciante, el beneficio clave es el precio.»

feedback.es: According to atribuye la idea a la fuente: es la señal básica de un resumen fiel.

hint.es: Dos palabras en total; la primera empieza por a.

origin.text: ___ to the lecturer, the key benefit of shared bikes is the price, and she went on to give a detail: one dollar per half hour.

prompt.es: Ordena: «Continuó dando un detalle revelador sobre el coste.»

answer.text: She went on to give a telling detail about the cost

feedback.es: Went on to + verbo añade un dato concreto después de la idea principal.

hint.es: El sujeto es she y el verbo frasal va antes del infinitivo.

prompt.es: Escucha y elige qué tema recurrente destaca la conferenciante.

choices.text: People ignore background sound more easily than speech.
Open offices are always noisier than private rooms.
Staff in call centres dislike wearing headphones.

feedback.es: El tema recurrente es que el sonido de fondo se tolera, pero el habla distrae; los auriculares son solo el ejemplo.

origin.audio: The lecturer began by saying that she would cover two topics. The first was noise in open offices; the second was light. On noise, she drew attention to a recurring theme in the research: people can get used to background sound, but they cannot easily ignore speech. By way of illustration, she mentioned a call centre where staff wore headphones.

prompt.es: Escucha y elige qué frase sería infiel en un resumen de la charla.

choices.text: Attendance doubles during the winter months.
Night classes are better than daytime classes.
At least one college runs them on three evenings a week.

feedback.es: La conferenciante dice que convienen a quien trabaja de día, que la asistencia se duplica en invierno y que un colegio los ofrece tres tardes por semana; nunca dice que sean mejores que los de día, así que esa frase sería infiel.

origin.audio: Night classes suit people who work during the day, the lecturer said, and attendance doubles in winter. For many adults they are the only option, and one college now runs them on three evenings a week.

prompt.es: Completa: «Cuando tomes apuntes, escribe cifras, nombres y palabras clave.»

feedback.es: Take notes es la colocación para tomar apuntes durante una charla.

origin.text: When you take ___, write numbers, names and keywords; whole sentences will make you fall behind.

prompt.es: Escucha la charla y resume tres ideas y dos detalles.

answer.text: The lecturer began by saying that she wanted to look at why some companies are trying a four-day working week, and she then outlined three main reasons. According to her, the first reason is that staff are more focused when a long weekend is coming, and the work done stayed the same at one firm in Bristol. The second reason is that sick days fell sharply, by about a third in a year. The third reason is that it became easier to recruit, because candidates see the shorter week as a sign of trust. By way of illustration, she described a company that reduced its hours from forty to thirty-two without cutting pay. She went on to draw attention to a limit: the change is not suitable for every kind of business, since hospitals and shops cannot simply close on Fridays. In short, the lecturer said that the four-day week works best where results, not hours, can be measured, and she did not suggest that every company should copy it.
accepted: The lecturer began by saying that she wanted to look at why some companies are trying a four-day working week, and she then outlined three main reasons. The second reason is that sick days fell sharply, by about a third in a year. The third reason is that it became easier to recruit, because candidates see the shorter week as a sign of trust. By way of illustration, she described a company that reduced its hours from forty to thirty-two without cutting pay. She went on to draw attention to a limit: the change is not suitable for every kind of business, since hospitals and shops cannot simply close on Fridays. In short, the lecturer said that the four-day week works best where results, not hours, can be measured, and she did not suggest that every company should copy it.

The talk was about why some companies are trying a four-day week, and the speaker gave three main ideas. Firstly, staff seem to be more focused when a long weekend is coming, and at one firm in Bristol the work done did not change. Secondly, sick days fell: they went down by roughly a third in a year. Thirdly, it was easier to recruit people, since candidates see a shorter week as a sign of trust. As an example, she explained that a company cut its hours from forty to thirty-two and did not reduce pay. She also pointed out a limit: the idea does not suit every kind of business, because hospitals and shops cannot close on Fridays. To sum up, according to the lecturer, the four-day week is best where results can be measured rather than hours, although she did not say that every company should copy it.

feedback.es: El resumen recoge las tres razones, al menos dos detalles, atribuye las ideas a la conferenciante, menciona el límite y cierra con una conclusión.

origin.text: Escucha la charla sobre la semana laboral de cuatro días (puedes oírla varias veces) y escribe un resumen en inglés de unas 170–250 palabras: tres ideas principales, dos detalles o ejemplos, un límite y una frase final. Atribuye las ideas a la conferenciante y no añadas datos que no oigas.
origin.audio: Good morning. Today I want to look at why some companies are trying a four-day working week. There are three main reasons. First, managers report that staff are more focused when they know a long weekend is coming, and one firm in Bristol found that the work done stayed the same after the change. Second, sick days fell sharply, by about a third in a year. Third, it became easier to recruit, because candidates see the shorter week as a sign of trust. By way of illustration, one company reduced its hours from forty to thirty-two without cutting pay. However, the change is not suitable for every kind of business; hospitals and shops cannot simply close on Fridays. In short, the four-day week works best where results can be measured, not hours.

prompt.es: Escucha la charla y elige por qué menciona hospitales y tiendas.

choices.text: To illustrate a company that cut its hours without cutting pay.
To explain why candidates see a shorter week as a sign of trust.
To show that the idea has limits in some kinds of business.

feedback.es: Los hospitales y las tiendas son el ejemplo del límite: no pueden cerrar los viernes, así que el cambio no sirve para todos los sectores; la empresa que redujo horas y la confianza de los candidatos son otros ejemplos de la charla.

feedback.es: By way of illustration (o by way of example) introduce un caso concreto que respalda la idea.

answer.text: The lecturer outlined three reasons and went on to give an example

prompt.es: ¿Qué ha aprendido el autor de su experiencia con los apuntes?

choices.text: That choosing key points matters more than copying everything.
That he should have recorded the talk and skipped the notes.
That shorter notes will make the summary less accurate.

feedback.es: Copiarlo todo no le sirvió para resumir; decide anotar solo cifras, nombres y un punto clave por parte, sin renunciar a tomar notas ni temer que el resumen pierda precisión.

origin.text: I copied every sentence the lecturer said, and my notes ran to six pages. Yet when I tried to summarise the talk, I could not tell which point mattered most. Next time I will write only the numbers, the names and one key point per section.

prompt.es: Escucha y elige qué insinúa la hablante sobre la fecha de apertura.

choices.text: That she trusts the council's confidence completely.
That she doubts the date will be met.
That the council has already changed the date.

feedback.es: Menciona plazos incumplidos y atribuye la confianza al municipio con «in its own words»: se distancia de esa confianza y da a entender que duda de que se cumpla marzo.

origin.audio: She said the new library would open in March, although the builders had already missed two deadlines, and then went on to say that the council was, in its own words, very confident.

prompt.es: Ordena: «Según la conferenciante, el punto clave es el coste.»

answer.text: According to the lecturer the key point is the cost

feedback.es: According to atribuye la idea y the key point is… presenta la idea principal.
